content: The administration of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs in pediatric populations is challenging due to the lack of comprehensive pharmacokinetic, safety, and dosing data, as well as the absence of suitable formulations. In the 2018 revision of the World Health Organization (WHO) ARV guidelines, integrase inhibitors were given a more prominent role among the preferred treatment regimens. At the time of this update, dolutegravir (DTG) was approved for use in children over 6 years of age and weighing at least 15 kg in Europe, and for children weighing over 30 kg in the United States. A registration trial was anticipated to provide dosing data for DTG in children as young as 4 weeks of age by early 2019, with potential regulatory approval expected later that year. The simplified dosing recommendations for DTG were based on preliminary pharmacokinetic and safety data from an ongoing multicountry study, which also investigated the pharmacokinetics of DTG in children co-treated for tuberculosis. These findings were expected to be confirmed in early 2019. Given the time required to introduce pediatric DTG, healthcare programs were encouraged to begin planning for its use in pediatric populations while awaiting confirmation of the simplified dosing. Raltegravir (RAL) granules were also introduced to provide a suitable formulation for neonates. However, due to concerns about the complexity of administering the granule formulation, the Pediatric Antiretroviral Working Group (PAWG) endorsed the use of 25 mg chewable tablets as dispersible tablets for infants and children older than 4 weeks and weighing at least 3 kg. This decision was based on in vitro data demonstrating solubility and bioequivalence between RAL tablets and granules, as well as the limited availability of alternative formulations for this age group. The dosing annex and simplified dosing schedules will be regularly reviewed and updated as new data and formulations become available. ARV drugs and formulations are produced by multiple manufacturers, and the available dosage strengths of tablets, capsules, and liquid formulations may vary. Several optimal pediatric dosage forms are under development but have not yet received regulatory approval. National program managers must ensure that products planned for use have received stringent regulatory approval and meet appropriate quality and stability standards. The WHO simplified tables for pediatric ARV dosing emphasize the use of age-appropriate fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) whenever available. Oral liquid or syrup formulations should be avoided when possible, with dispersible tablets or granules for oral solution being the preferred solid oral dosage forms. If suitable dispersible FDCs are unavailable, children should be transitioned to solid oral dosage forms as soon as possible. Neonates often require oral liquid formulations for precise dosing, but switching to solid oral dosage forms is recommended as soon as feasible. When adult formulations are used for children, care must be taken to avoid under-dosing or overdosing, and scored tablets are preferred to ensure accurate dosing. Splitting unscored tablets should be avoided due to the risk of uneven distribution of the active drug. Certain tablets, such as heat-stable lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) or atazanavir (ATV) tablets, are manufactured using proprietary melt extrusion technology to stabilize heat-labile drug molecules. These tablets must not be cut, split, dissolved, chewed, or crushed, as this significantly reduces bioavailability. At each clinical visit, children should be weighed, and doses should be adjusted based on observed growth and changes in body weight. National programs should consider the regulatory and local availability status of specific dosage forms when developing pediatric treatment recommendations. Research is ongoing to establish dosing guidance for several ARV medications in neonates, infants, and young children. Age indications for each drug are based on current evidence and will be updated as new recommendations become available. For infants younger than 4 weeks, dosing is reduced to account for their decreased ability to excrete and metabolize medications. For infants at least 4 weeks old but weighing less than 3 kg, renal and hepatic immaturity is less of a concern, but uncertainty remains regarding appropriate dosing in preterm and low birth weight infants. Nevirapine (NVP) dose escalation with a half-dose for 2 weeks when initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) is still recommended to avoid toxicity from high initial NVP levels. However, secondary analysis from the CHAPAS-1 trial suggests that younger children have a lower risk of toxicity, and starting with a full dose may be considered. More definitive evidence is expected from ongoing trials. It is important to note that this regimen and formulation are no longer recommended and should only be used in special circumstances where other age-appropriate formulations are unavailable. LPV/r liquid requires a cold chain for transport and storage. The heat-stable LPV/r tablet formulation must be swallowed whole and should not be split, chewed, dissolved, or crushed. LPV/r pellets should not be used in infants younger than 3 months. This dosing schedule applies to equivalent solid dosage forms that may become available in the near future, such as granules. RAL granules are approved for use from birth. However, the feasibility and acceptability of such formulations have not been widely investigated, and concerns have been raised regarding administration in resource-limited settings. Due to the challenges associated with administering the granule formulation, the use of 25 mg chewable tablets as dispersible tablets has been endorsed by the PAWG for infants and children older than 4 weeks and weighing at least 3 kg. This recommendation was based on in vitro data on solubility and bioequivalence between tablets and granules, as well as the limited availability of adequate alternatives for this age group. Findings from a feasibility and acceptability assessment conducted in South Africa indicate that administering RAL granules in rural settings is feasible with adequate training and counseling support.
